html:
SMTO-AUT-0013 — SMTO couldn't complete sign-in with the service

GUID: c1a51cbb-fe1c-5e89-a8d9-3fa61a98df5c
Slug: auth-provider-unreachable
Domain: AUT · Subsystem: auth-broker

What happened

  • SMTO tried to reach the service's sign-in system but couldn't, or got back an answer it couldn't use or trust. The sign-in wasn't completed.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. Check whether the service is having problems, for example on its status page, and wait until it's working normally. If the service's sign-in system is down or failing, SMTO can't finish signing in.
  2. Make sure the computer running SMTO is online. For email connections, also check that the selected Gateway is online in Settings › Setup › Gateways. Sign-in requests go out from SMTO's computer, or from the Gateway for email, so that machine must reach the service.
  3. Ask the person who manages SMTO to check the connection's sign-in addresses in Parameter Store and whether your network needs a proxy. SMTO only trusts the sign-in addresses saved for the connection and doesn't use system proxy settings for this step.
  4. Once the service is reachable, check whether the step already made its change, then ask SMTO in the conversation to try it again. Checking first avoids repeating a change that may already have happened.

What success looks like

  • The sign-in finishes with Authorization complete, or the step continues without this error.

If it still fails

  • Select Copy error details and send them to the person who manages SMTO. Don't turn off security checks or add unfamiliar sign-in addresses to get around this.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • An OAuth exchange or discovery request failed: the HTTPS request errored or timed out, the endpoint returned an unexpected status or provider error, or discovery advertised an endpoint outside the issuer and trusted_endpoint_origins.

What this means

  • OAuth transport failed, returned an unsupported status/provider error, or discovery supplied an endpoint outside the configured trusted origins. Authorization establishes a particular connection, account and scope. It neither expands operation permissions nor proves the outcome of a request already dispatched.

Why this can happen

  • OAuth transport failed, returned an unsupported status/provider error, or discovery supplied an endpoint outside the configured trusted origins.

How to diagnose it

  • Distinguish connectivity failure from response status and discovery-origin rejection before changing endpoint configuration.

How to fix it

  • From the host that performs the exchange (the Server, or the selected Gateway for email OAuth), test HTTPS reachability of the issuer's discovery document and token endpoint; the OAuth transport ignores proxy environment variables and does not follow redirects. Fix DNS, firewall or provider issues, and add an endpoint origin to the client's trusted_endpoint_origins only if it genuinely belongs to the provider.
  • Check trusted HTTPS endpoints, response status and discovery configuration; repair the specific failure before restarting authorization.

Retry and execution caution

  • Correct the reported condition and check delivery evidence before starting another operation.

How to verify the fix

  • The configured trusted endpoint returns an accepted bounded response for the intended exchange.

What not to do

  • Do not expose passwords, access tokens, authorization codes or SMTP authentication payloads.
  • Do not automatically repeat an operation whose remote effect is unknown.

Technical notes

  • Authorization establishes a particular connection, account and scope. It neither expands operation permissions nor proves the outcome of a request already dispatched.
  • Preserve the occurrence ID and safe request/operation references. Receipts and occurrence facts establish what started or completed; the catalog does not authorize retries or establish execution outcome.
